section_summary: Most of this section consists of hundreds of signatures on a petition addressed to President Franklin D. Roosevelt and Secretary of State Cordell Hull, protesting exports of scrap iron and other war materials to Japan. It also contains letters and resolutions from religious leaders, missionaries, academics, and peace organizations urging embargoes or stronger action against Japanese aggression in China, together with State Department acknowledgments explaining the limits of the Neutrality Act. The closing documents concern consultations with Britain over restricting aircraft, oil, steel, credit, and other supplies to Japan.

subfiles.title: Petition sheets protesting exports of scrap iron and war materials to Japan, first group
subfiles.from: Petition signatories gathered by the Peace Committee and associated San Diego peace activists
subfiles.to: Franklin D. Roosevelt and Cordell Hull
subfiles.about: Residents principally of San Diego County, with some signers from Yuma and other communities, protest the shipment of scrap iron and other war materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: These pages continue a standardized petition asking President Roosevelt and Secretary Hull to stop exports of scrap iron and other war material to Japan. Each sheet carries handwritten names, street addresses, and cities, most of them in the San Diego area. The repeated footer directs completed petitions to the Peace Committee at 3546 First Avenue, San Diego.

subfiles.title: Letter forwarding 1,015 petition signatures
subfiles.from: Kate H. Kling, for the Women's International League for Peace and Freedom and the San Diego Peace Committee
subfiles.to: Cordell Hull, attention C. W. Grist, Assistant Chief, Office of Arms and Munitions Control
subfiles.about: The San Diego peace organizations forward 1,015 signatures opposing the shipment of scrap iron to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Handwritten letter encloses 1,015 petition signatures against sending scrap iron to Japan, sponsored by the Women's International League and San Diego Peace Committee.
keywords: Women's International League for Peace and Freedom

subfiles.title: Petition sheets protesting exports of scrap iron and war materials to Japan, second group
subfiles.from: Petition signatories gathered by the Peace Committee and associated peace organizations
subfiles.to: Franklin D. Roosevelt and Cordell Hull
subfiles.about: Additional signatories urge the administration to stop exports of scrap iron and other war materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: These further standardized sheets contain hundreds of signatures and addresses from San Diego County and other places, including Yuma, Julian, Los Angeles, Hollywood, and nearby California communities. The text of every sheet protests the shipment of scrap iron and other war material to Japan. The forms again direct completed petitions to the Peace Committee in San Diego.

subfiles.title: Women's Auxiliary of Congaree Presbytery resolution on war materials for Japan
subfiles.from: I. M. Keels and J. R. West, Woman's Auxiliary of Congaree Presbytery
subfiles.about: The organization forwards a resolution supporting efforts to curb shipments to Japan that could aid its invasion of China.
subfiles.summary: Business Women's Conference of Congaree Presbytery approves a YWCA resolution urging limits on materials directly useful to Japan's invasion of China, noting U.S. importance as Japanese-goods consumer and war-material exporter.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to I. M. Keels on the Neutrality Act
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The State Department explains why the Neutrality Act had not been invoked against China and Japan and supplies arms-export totals.
subfiles.summary: Green tells I. M. Keels a war finding would embargo arms to China and Japan, the law doesn't authorize restricting other goods, and licensed arms exports since July 1, 1937 were $14,267,823.21 to China and $10,793,885.38 to Japan; Act and pamphlet enclosed.

subfiles.title: Christine S. Chambers urges an economic embargo against Japan
subfiles.about: A missionary and Shanghai university teacher praises American consular personnel in China and urges the government to stop all economic and financial aid to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Christine Chambers, after twenty-four years' missionary service in China, supports the Open Door, says American supplies enable Japanese aggression, and calls for an enforceable economic and financial embargo.

subfiles.title: J. Leighton Stuart appeals for stronger American action in China
subfiles.about: Stuart describes Japanese occupation and atrocities in China and urges mediation, an embargo, or other forceful American action.
subfiles.summary: J. Leighton Stuart thanks Roosevelt, describes Japanese looting, killing and plans for permanent control of North China, warns against a settlement leaving Japan dominant, says an embargo wouldn't risk war, and offers to accept risks to American lives and property.

subfiles.title: Instruction to the American Embassy at Peiping concerning Stuart's letter
subfiles.about: The Department sends Stuart's letter to the embassy and requests an acknowledgment on President Roosevelt's behalf.
subfiles.summary: Instruction to Peiping encloses Stuart's October 15 reply; unless objected to, tell him Roosevelt received it and considered it carefully; copy for Chongqing.

subfiles.title: Quincy Wright urges a coordinated embargo against Japan
subfiles.about: Wright advocates legislation and international coordination to embargo war materials, petroleum, metals, and loans to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Quincy Wright, answering Walter Lippmann, says China's collapse and British accommodation are overstated, proposes congressional authority for an embargo on copper, iron, petroleum and loans, then talks with Britain, France and other Nine-Power states, and urges Anglo-American cooperation.

subfiles.title: State Department acknowledgment to Quincy Wright
subfiles.from: R. Walton Moore, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department acknowledges Wright's letter and promises careful consideration of his views on the Far East.
subfiles.summary: Moore thanks Wright for his November 8 letter; the Department welcomes thoughtful public opinion and weighs it with other factors.

subfiles.title: White House referral to the State Department
subfiles.from: Marvin H. McIntyre, Secretary to the President
subfiles.about: The White House refers incoming correspondence concerning Japan and China to the State Department.
subfiles.summary: White House referral slip, signed by Marvin McIntyre, sending the attached matter to State, file 894.24/451.

subfiles.title: Forwarding letter for the Batesville ministers' resolution
subfiles.from: John E. Miller, probable identification; signature unclear in OCR
subfiles.about: The sender forwards a resolution adopted by ministers in Batesville, Arkansas, at the request of J. A. Gatlin.
subfiles.summary: Forwarding letter encloses a Batesville ministers' resolution for the President, as requested by Rev. J. A. Gatlin, secretary.

subfiles.title: Resolution of the ministers of Batesville against supplying Japan
subfiles.from: J. A. Gatlin, secretary, for the ministers of Batesville, Arkansas
subfiles.about: Batesville ministers ask Roosevelt to stop sales of oil, aircraft, munitions, and other war-useful commodities to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Batesville ministers implore the President to halt sales of oil, airplanes and munitions to Japan to help close its war on the Chinese people.

subfiles.title: British Embassy aide-mémoire concerning parallel action against Japan
subfiles.about: Britain asks for details of American measures affecting aircraft sales and credit to Japan after a Chinese diplomatic approach in London.
subfiles.summary: British aide-memoire: the Chinese Ambassador asked Britain to implement League commitments by embargo or pressure on manufacturers; the British Ambassador asks details of U.S. action on aircraft sales and credit so Britain can consider parallel measures.

subfiles.title: State Department reply on aircraft exports and commercial credit to Japan
subfiles.about: The Department explains American policies discouraging aircraft exports useful for bombing civilians and warning exporters about Japanese exchange restrictions.
subfiles.summary: State reply: Hull's June 11 bombing condemnation reached aircraft makers and exporters, who were warned licenses would be regretted for offenders; a Commerce circular advises irrevocable letters of credit for Japan. Continues past page 224.
